query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX HEAs exposed to temperatures above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres, the formation and persistence of a stable, coherent protective oxide layer are determined by the identity of the X element. When X is Al or Si, the element preferentially oxidizes to form dense, low-mismatch oxides (i.e. alumina or silica) that adhere strongly to the substrate, while when X is Mn, the resulting oxide is non-protective, prone to cracking or spallation due to higher oxidation rates and volatility.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy in either a single- or multiphase metallic solid solution state, with baseline comparison using the Mn-containing alloy (CrFeCoNiMn).
generation.intervention: Expose the HEA samples to temperatures above 900 °C in a controlled oxidative (or specified corrosive) environment.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure (>900 °C) in either air or a well-defined corrosive atmosphere (e.g., molten salt environments) under identical thermal cycling and exposure durations.
generation.structural_mediator: The chemical composition and lattice coherence (i.e. misfit strain) at the metal–oxide interface, which governs the adhesion and integrity of the oxide layer.
generation.mechanism: Element-specific oxidation behavior: Al and Si, due to favorable oxidation thermodynamics and slower diffusion in the alloy matrix, form stable, coherent, and low-mismatch oxide layers that act as effective barriers. In contrast, Mn oxidizes more rapidly to form volatile or poorly adherent oxides that crack or spall, thereby failing to protect the underlying alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys where X = Al or Si will develop and maintain a continuous, coherent protective oxide layer with minimal spallation, whereas alloys where X = Mn will display unstable oxide scales that crack and spall during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
generation.baseline: The CrFeCoNiMn high-entropy alloy, which is expected to form an unstable, non-protective oxide layer under the same high-temperature oxidative conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies only to high-entropy alloys in single- or multiphase solid solution states, exposed to temperatures above 900 °C in defined oxidative or corrosive environments; effects of other processing variables or lower temperature regimes are not accounted for.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the quantitative role of multiphase microstructures on the diffusion kinetics and oxide layer coherence, as well as the potential influence of other minor alloying elements on the oxidation mechanism.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of CrFeCoNiX HEA specimens where X is varied between Mn (baseline), Al, and Si while keeping the other elements constant. Expose all specimens to a controlled high-temperature environment (>900 °C) in air (or in a defined corrosive medium) for a fixed duration. Use identical processing histories to ensure consistent microstructures. Monitor oxide scale formation in situ (e.g., via high-temperature X-ray diffraction) and post-exposure using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) to assess continuity, adherence, and spallation of the oxide layer.
measurements: In situ XRD for phase identification during high-temperature exposure
SEM imaging of the oxide scale morphology and evidence of cracking/spallation
EDS for compositional analysis of the oxide layer
Weight gain measurements as an indirect measure of oxidation kinetics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al- or Si-containing alloys do not show a statistically significant improvement in the continuity, adherence, and protective nature of the oxide layer (as measured by reduced spallation, more coherent morphology, and controlled oxidation kinetics) compared to the Mn-containing baseline, then the hypothesis that the identity of the X element controls the protective oxide formation via the proposed mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.
